lines.note: Joozukai is a person designated for errands or business, paraphrased by sadamaritaru tsukai. The final de begins determinada on the next row without a printed hyphen.
Terminada completes the adjective and the gloss specifies messages or other business. This continues the appointed-messenger entry anticipated by f0255's catchword.

runs.text: O eſtar ſempre em caſa do ſenhor

lines.note: Joozume means remaining continuously at the lord's house. The description of readiness and its Japanese example follow on the next row.
The attendant stays ready for everything; joozume shite iru illustrates the state. The capital is G, not OCR Cri, and the printed close spacing peratudo is retained.
Juu is illustrated by juu suru and glossed with sumu, residing. The caroned u is visible in both occurrences; Vt belongs to the italic apparatus.
Morar completes the Portuguese pair estar ou morar, being or dwelling. The one-word row belongs to Giǔ and is not an independent entry.

runs.text: Caixa repartida ẽ tres, ou mais pe-

lines.note: Juubako is a box divided into three or more sections. The printed abbreviation ẽ and the division pe- / ças are retained.

runs.text: ças hũas ſobre outras de maneira que pareça

lines.note: The sections are stacked one above another so that the whole appears to be one object. This describes the arrangement of the tiered box rather than separate unrelated containers.
Hũa ſoo completes the explanation that the stacked sections appear to form a single box. Preserve the old spelling and the printed tilde.
Juubon is a grave fault or sin, paraphrased as omoi toga. The scan supports Giǔbon and i, instead of the OCR's garbled Cifibon and stop.
Ve completes grave, and pecado identifies the fault as sin. The line closes the Juubon entry.
Juubuku is explained by kasane kiru, wearing in layers. The Portuguese starts with putting one garment over another; the headword's worn u is retained.

runs.text: ſobre outro, ou veſtido forrado, & eſtofado.

lines.note: Completes the layered-clothing definition and adds lined, padded clothing. The printed eſtofado is preserved without modernization.

runs.text: O não ſair por cerimonia, ou agou

lines.note: A separate Juubuku concerns not going outside through ceremonial observance or concern about omens. The final agou continues into agouro below without an added hyphen.

runs.text: ro quando ha pouco que morreo o pay, ou parẽ-

lines.note: The observance follows the recent death of a father or relative. The line-end parẽ- bears an abbreviation tilde and continues as te, rather than losing the nasal consonant in interpretation.
Te completes parẽte, and dalguem closes the phrase about someone's relative. This is the mourning-related Juubuku, not the preceding clothing entry.
Juukoku means residence in a realm, paraphrased by kuni ni sumu. The Portuguese has aßento; the OCR added a redundant long s after the double-s sort.
No reino completes the explanation of settled residence in the kingdom or territory. It is not an additional Japanese equivalent.
Juudai concerns successive ages or generations, paraphrased by kasanuru yo. Idades is not divided internally; Vt introduces a hereditary-service example.
Juudai no hikan denotes a retainer whose service extends over generations. The u bears a caron, not the OCR grave; antiguo is the source's historical spelling.
Idades completes the reference to service over many generations. The row belongs to the hereditary-retainer example rather than to a new entry.

runs.text: Couſa repetida por eſcrito, ou eſcri-

lines.note: Juuden is something repeated in writing or written twice. The alternative wording continues after the printed eſcri-.
Ta completes escrita and duas vezes explicitly gives the twice-written sense. This is the end of the written-repetition entry.
Juuji is the superior of a monastery or temple. The Portuguese institutional terms moeſteiro and varela are retained rather than replaced with a modern title.
Juugon denotes repeated words, paraphrased by kasanuru kotoba. The Portuguese repetidas is divided after repe-.
Tidas completes repetidas, with ditas duas vezes making the repetition explicit. This row closes Juugon.
Juujuu is glossed by kasanegasane, repeatedly. The Portuguese begins once and again, divided after ou-.

runs.text: tra. ¶ Item, Degraos, ou graos de hon-

lines.note: Tra completes outra. An additional sense concerns steps or degrees of honours and virtues; hon- continues on the next row.
Ras completes honras, followed by virtues and other graded qualities. This continues the second sense of Juujuu.
Juu-i concerns increasing or accumulating rank, paraphrased by kurai wo kasanuru. The internal hyphen is lexical separation of i, not a line-end division.

runs.text: grao auẽtajado ſobre outro. ¶ Item, Per

lines.note: The rank or degree is advanced above another; the following Per begins the metaphorical usage label. Auẽtajado retains the printed abbreviation tilde.

runs.text: met. Ventajem, ou exceßo em letras, ou em

lines.note: Met completes Per met. The metaphorical sense is superiority or excellence in learning, with another field of skill specified on the next row; Ventajem is retained as printed.
Completes the metaphorical sense as excellence in some other art or skill. This final continuation still belongs to Giǔ-i.
Juumot is an object handed down over generations, explicitly paraphrased by juudai ni tsutawaru mono. Portuguese couſa is divided after Cou with no visible hyphen.
Sa completes couſa, describing an old object of many generations. The next example begins with Juumot and continues into ni mono wo suru.
Juumot ni mono wo suru is used metaphorically for making something durable. Permet. is an explanatory label, not Japanese text.

runs.text: couſa que dure por muito tempo. ¶

lines.note: Completes the translation as making something last a long time, then begins a second example with the divided Giǔ-.
Motna mono completes the adjectival phrase for a durable thing. The source's checked t before na is preserved instead of being expanded to modern spelling.
The object is made or arranged to endure a long time. This closes the second example of Juumot.
Juuni is glossed as two pips or points on dice. The Portuguese põtos keeps its abbreviation tilde; the explanation concerns a dice term rather than supplying a general numeral definition.
Juunin is a resident, paraphrased as sumu hito. The damaged initial is G, not OCR Cri; Mia- begins the example about a resident of the capital.
Kono joins Mia- to form Miyako no juunin, a resident of the principal city. The Portuguese translation explicitly identifies the chief city.
Ou corte adds the alternative description as the court or capital. This continuation closes the resident example.
Juukyo is settled residence, paraphrased with the visibly punctuated Sumi, iru. The Portuguese aßẽto retains its double-s sort and nasal abbreviation.
Juukyo suru is the verbal example, residing or taking up residence. It has no additional Portuguese translation on this short row.
Juukwa denotes a grave fault or sin, with omoi toga as the Japanese paraphrase. The capital is G rather than OCR C.
Juukwanin is a person guilty of grave sin. The gloss's doubled cc in peccador is preserved independently of the single-c pecado on the preceding row.
Juusoo names resident Buddhist monks, paraphrased as sumu hijiri. The scan supports the worn Giǔſô, not OCR Giiſô; the gloss continues with their place of residence.
Completes the explanation as monks residing in a monastery. This is a continuation of Juusoo and not a separate institutional entry.
Juutaku concerns inhabiting a house or dwelling, paraphrased by sumu iye. The Portuguese da- starts the contracted expression for settled residence, continued below.
The continuation reads ſẽto, completing the settled-residence expression. Its faint nasal abbreviation is retained, and the gloss allows residence in any place.
Juuon denotes accumulated or repeated benefactions, paraphrased by kasanaru megumi. The damaged headword reads Giǔuon, not OCR Gifuon; the Portuguese adjective continues below.
Completes the gloss as great and numerous benefits. This closes the benefaction entry rather than the subsequent mountain-residence entry.
Juusen is glossed by yama ni sumu, living in the mountains. Portuguese mõtes retains the nasal abbreviation rather than spelling out the missing n.
Juushi, with the printed principal forms uru and ita, is to inhabit or reside. The opening capital is G, not OCR C; preserve the supplied abbreviated inflection pattern.
Juusho is a dwelling place, paraphrased by sumidokoro. The Portuguese noun is lugar, not the OCR's lagar, which would change the meaning.
Completes the definition as the place where one lives. This is the first, dwelling-place Juusho entry.

runs.text: Giǔxo. i, Iyeni tçutauaru xo. L

lines.note: A second Juusho is a book passed down within a household, paraphrased by ie ni tsutawaru sho. The repeated headword is a distinct entry, not accidental duplication.

runs.text: vem por deſcendencia em algũa familia a cer-

lines.note: The book descends through a family. The phrase a cer- continues into the subject matter recorded in it; its physical division is retained.
Completes a cerca and identifies family lineage, rents, or similar matters as the book's contents. The printed mark in gèração is retained.
Juushoku is an office, charge, or dignity transmitted through generations. The headword has no extra i before x, and Portuguese ou is a single word.

runs.text: vem continuandoſe por idades nos pays, fi-

lines.note: The office continues through fathers and descendants. The visible line-end fi- begins filhos; OCR lost the i, while the worn nos is still recoverable.

runs.text: lhos, netos, &c. ¶ Item, Officio, ou car-

lines.note: Lhos completes filhos, followed by grandchildren. An additional sense begins with an office or charge, divided after car-.

runs.text: go annexo a algũa dignidade ẽ caſa do Dairi

lines.note: Go completes cargo: an office attached to a dignity in the Dairi's household or court. Dairi is a Japanese institutional term embedded in the Portuguese sentence and is set apart in roman type.
A visible paragraph sign introduces another Juushoku sense, paraphrased by omoi kurai. The headword is Giǔxocu, not OCR Ciixocu; Grã- starts the Portuguese grande.

runs.text: de, ou auentajada dignidade, ou cargo.

lines.note: De completes grande, describing a high or eminent dignity or office. This closes the set of Juushoku explanations.
Juuyaku concerns additional or multiple duties, paraphrased as kasanaru yaku. Officio is one word; acrecen- continues the description below.
Tado completes acrecentado, with many offices given as an alternative formulation. This belongs to the cumulative-duty entry.
Another Juuyaku is simply identified as the name of a plant. No species identification is supplied in the line, so none is inserted into the transcription or interpretation.
Juuyen is kinship through multiple connections. The source reads muitas vias, not OCR muitar; the example follows on the next row.

runs.text: o que caſa hum filho e filha com dous irmãos

lines.note: The example marries a son and a daughter to two siblings. Irmãos restores a weak r rather than treating the OCR's i mãos as separate words.

runs.text: ficando conſogro do outro por duas vias.

lines.note: The two parents thereby become co-parents-in-law through two marriages. This completes the example of multiple kinship links and does not refer to the married pair becoming siblings.
Juuzai is a grave sin, paraphrased by omoi tsumi. The visible headword is Giǔzai, with worn marked u, not OCR Gibzai.
Juuzainin is a person guilty of grave sin. This closes the G-before-I section before the independent letter-I heading and decorated initial.

zones.label: Column 2, part 2
zones.note: Decorated initial I spans the first six body rows.

lines.note: The decorated I is the actual headword, meaning imposing presence or majesty. Its ornament spans six physical rows; no independent stop after the initial is visible. The OCR omitted the headword while retaining its Portuguese gloss.
The example begins kunshi omokarazaru: when a cultivated or wise person lacks gravity. Vt is italic; the Japanese statement continues on the next row beside the initial.

Toki wa i arazu completes the statement that such a person lacks authority or awe. Retain the printed space after the internal hyphen; prudẽ continues into Portuguese prudente without an added line-end mark.

runs.text: te, & ſabio quando não he gra

lines.note: Te completes prudente, and sabio reinforces the wise person's description. Gra begins grave on the next row, again without a supplied hyphen.
Ve completes grave: without gravity he has no power or authority. The row is indented beside the large initial; autori- visibly continues into dade below.

Dade completes autoridade, then I no aru hito describes a person who possesses that imposing presence. The source has a space after I; OCR Gz at the beginning came from the initial's decorative border, not running letters.
The person is glossed as possessing authority and majesty. This is the first full-width continuation beneath the decorated initial.
I wo furuu illustrates displaying power or imposing presence. Restore the visible paragraph sign and the separate capital I before uo; OCR luo misread and joined them.

runs.text: Medico. Não ſe vſa, ſe não ẽ

lines.note: A new I entry means physician, with kusushi as its Japanese equivalent. The gloss says that this I is not used except in compounds; the headword is capital I, not lowercase l.
The compound mei-i means an excellent physician. The lexical hyphen is printed inside the Japanese example and is not a physical line-break marker.
Tai-i is another compound, glossed as a great physician. This row remains part of the physician entry.
A separate I means a well. I wo horu is digging a well; the capital I and its following space replace the OCR's Auo, and the last Portuguese poço is worn but usable.

runs.text: Fel, mas não ſe vſa ſem compoſição. Vt,

lines.note: The next I means gall or bile, restricted here to compounds. The source uses the close spacing nãoſe and introduces an example with italic Vt.

Kuma no i is bear gall. The Portuguese word after do appears as vco in this damaged impression; retain that provisional visible reading rather than silently replacing it with expected urso or another historical spelling.
The final I entry is rush or reed. Imuxiro illustrates a rush mat, matched by Eſteira de junco; the isolated headword is capital I rather than the OCR lowercase i.
